/v/askgoat actually does have rules now. Except they are for the mods and are designed to prevent mod abuse.

I'm not a fan of rules for mods, and this is why:

Ordinarily, mods have zero power in removing posts except what power is granted by sub rules. With rules for mods, the implication is that mods have unlimited power except where limited by sub rules.

I understand having set policy for user bans and post removals, but the approach should be "no power unless X", not "no limits except X".
If there are no rules, what stops mods from removing everything? You could easily create a sub with no rules and arbitrarily remove posts as you see fit. It would be too chaotic.

Nothing stops mods from ignoring rules they set for themselves either. You either trust both systems or neither. I just think the better approach is to start with zero and add, not start with everything and limit.

That said, I don't at all disagree with what you're doing with the sub and I wish you success, I just think we have a philosophical difference in how we view rule systems.

That's what rule 3 is for. If a user finds that a mod is not following these rules, they can submit a petition, with legitimate proof, calling for a vote of no confidence against the mod. This ensures that the mods must follow the rules, or else be kicked out. The users don't pick the new mods so there is no problem of popularity contests forming either.

That's a good system, but it still relies on mods holding up their end of the social contract. There's no outside force compelling them to comply. I do think it's a good system, and I do trust that social contract, but it's the same system that we already have, just inverted.

If I assume that mods have no power unless listed in the rules, the implication is that mods can't take action unless specified by a sub rule. Rules are powers, and removing a post that doesn't break a rule sparks outcry because it's abuse of power. When a situation comes along that we don't have a rule for, mods are powerless until a rule is established.

If I assume that mods have all power unless restricted by the rules, the implication is that mods can take action unless limited by their rules. Rules are restrictions, and removing a post that conflicts with those restrictions sparks outcry because it's abuse of power. When a situation comes along that we don't have a rule for, the mod is free to act until a rule is established.

Both systems rely on social contracts, but approach the idea of mod power from different sides of the spectrum. I'd rather consider mods powerless (enforced by social contract) unable to take action outside of enforcing sub rules. Having rules to strip power away from mods assumes they begin with power and can act outside those limits freely.

It's a lot like most governments. People have rights, government has powers. Government has no power unless granted by law. In the absence of law, government has no power. People have rights unless limited by law. In the absence of law, people's rights are absolute. It's still only a social contract and requires government to observe it, but it's a good system.

The outside forces are the users. The users still have the right to visit any sub they wish. Moderators have a vested interest in keeping their subs active with multiple users. If they break the social contract, they risk losing users to another subverse with mods willing to uphold the contract. As such, if they were presented with an agreement where they promise to obey the laws, it would be against their interests to break them.

This is true of both systems. I guess what I'm trying to convey is that I'd rather have a list of things that mods are allowed to do, with the assumption being that mods are powerless to act outside of that list. I prefer that over a list of restrictions that mods can't do, with the assumption being that mods can do whatever they want outside of those restrictions.

Many of your mod rules are already phrased like powers, not restrictions:

Moderators can only remove posts that either violate Voat's rules, create spam, or does not create absolutely any discussion at all.

The above is an example of a power, not a restriction. The following is a restriction:

If we must ban a user, two of the mods must be in agreement.

This doesn't really address what you can ban a user for, and the assumption is that you can ban users for anything as long as you don't violate the restriction.

I'd rather see something like:

Mods have the power to ban users that [criteria here] when [two mods are in agreement]

This directly addresses what you have the power to ban users for, under what circumstances, and the assumption is that you cannot ban users outside of the listed criteria.

Then if a situation arises that you don't have the power to address, the powers are revised and everything is done transparently and with due process.

If a situation arises that you don't have a restriction for, mods are free to take whatever action they want until a restriction is added. That's the reason why our government has powers and not restrictions, because an entity in power is more likely to add power when needed than it is to add restrictions when needed. Starting with zero is safer for the community.
